title: Partner deep dive: Splunk HEC recommendations + Redwood audit export field mapping
next_steps: Redwood to share draft Splunk sourcetype recommendation and example SPL queries for common audit scenarios (logins, API key rotation, RBAC changes).
ApexLogix to review mapping to Splunk CIM (Authentication/Change) and propose minimal field aliasing to avoid index-time transforms.
Redwood to confirm HEC ACK default behavior for the beta connector and document recommended HEC settings (ACK enabled, SSL/TLS, max batch sizing).
Schedule a 30-min follow-up once Redwood has the v1 schema examples finalized for export_config_change and rbac_change events.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript Export

Meeting: Partner deep dive: Splunk HEC recommendations + Redwood audit export field mapping
Date: 2025-01-29
Start time: 18:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes

Attendees
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood Inference)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference)
- Fatima Noor (Redwood Inference)
- Jordan Lee (ApexLogix)
- Maya Patel (ApexLogix)
- Evan Brooks (ApexLogix)

Summary (auto-generated)
- Reviewed Redwood’s SIEM-ready audit export (beta) and how events land in Splunk via HEC.
- Discussed recommended HEC settings (ACK, batching limits, TLS, token/index scoping) and operational failure modes.
- Walked through parsing guidance: JSON mode, sourcetype strategy, time extraction, and avoiding heavy index-time transforms.
- Partner provided field mapping suggestions to align with Splunk CIM for Authentication and Change/Configuration.

Topics
- HEC endpoint + auth token handling
- HEC ACK vs non-ACK delivery semantics
- Batching, event sizing, and backoff behavior
- Sourcetype naming + JSON field extraction
- CIM-ish field mapping + recommended aliases
- Dedupe guidance (at-least-once)

Action items (auto-generated)
- Colin: Send ApexLogix a one-pager with Redwood’s proposed Splunk sourcetype, host/source values, and example SPL.
- Kevin: Confirm which fields are always present in schema v1 and share a “minimum guaranteed” field list for correlation.
- Jordan: Provide a proposed CIM mapping table (search-time) for Redwood audit events, including required field aliases.

---

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Colin from Redwood. We pulled Kevin in who’s been leading the SIEM export security side, and Fatima who’s been on the regulated customers.

[00:11] Jordan Lee: Yep, good to meet. Jordan, ApexLogix, we do a lot of Splunk onboarding and parsing work. Maya and Evan are also on.

[00:19] Maya Patel: Hey everyone.

[00:20] Evan Brooks: Hi.

[00:22] Colin O'Donnell: The goal today is basically: we’re shipping a beta audit export with initial sinks being Splunk HEC, Datadog logs, and S3. We want to make sure Splunk lands cleanly and customers don’t have to do heroic transforms. Also, we’re at-least-once, so duplicates are possible, and we want your take on best practices.

[00:43] Jordan Lee: Makes sense. We can get pretty far with good sourcetype, JSON extraction, and a small set of field aliases. And for duplicates, consistent event IDs is the biggest thing.

[00:53] Kevin Osei: Yep, we have a stable event_id and also request_id-ish fields. We can talk about what you’d key on.

[01:01] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect. Maybe we start with HEC settings. Jordan, if you’re onboarding a vendor feed into Splunk, what do you recommend folks do with HEC?

[01:12] Jordan Lee: So, baseline: use HEC token scoped to an index dedicated for security logs, like index=security or index=prod_sec depending. If it’s Splunk Cloud, still same concept. Use TLS only. Enable HEC ACK if the sender supports it, especially if you care about delivery guarantees.

[01:28] Colin O'Donnell: We do support optional ACK. We’re still finalizing if it’s on by default in beta.

[01:33] Jordan Lee: If you can, default to ACK. Without ACK you’ll see the “it said 200 OK but it didn’t index” debates. ACK reduces that ambiguity.

[01:42] Kevin Osei: When you say ACK, you mean Splunk’s indexer acknowledgment where you post events and then poll ackId until committed, right?

[01:49] Jordan Lee: Exactly. /services/collector/event with the header for the token, and Splunk returns ackId. Then you hit /services/collector/ack. And you want to bound how long you wait.

[02:01] Evan Brooks: Also: in Splunk Cloud, depending on the stack, there can be some latency with ACK. So batching plus ACK polling can get chatty.

[02:11] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, that was one of our concerns. Our exporter is queue + worker based. We can do a batch, get ackIds, then poll. But we don’t want to DOS the HEC endpoint.

[02:22] Jordan Lee: Right. Rule of thumb: keep batch sizes reasonable. Don’t send like 10MB payloads. Also set a max in-flight batches per destination.

[02:32] Kevin Osei: What’s “reasonable” in your experience? We’ve been testing with like 200 events per batch or 512KB-ish.

[02:39] Jordan Lee: 200 events is fine if each event is small. I usually guide clients: cap request payload ~500KB to 1MB, and cap individual event around, I don’t know, 50KB to be safe. You’ll get weird failures if you send giant nested JSON.

[02:55] Maya Patel: And if you’re including stack traces, like error events, those can balloon.

[03:00] Kevin Osei: Our audit events shouldn’t include stack traces. We do include a “reason” field sometimes and some target metadata, but we’ve got PII redaction.

[03:08] Colin O'Donnell: We’ve also got a hard allowlist for fields in the export path, so it should be consistent.

[03:14] Jordan Lee: Good. Another HEC setting: set a consistent sourcetype. People get tempted to use sourcetype=_json but that’s not a best practice. Better is something like sourcetype=redwood:audit.

[03:28] Colin O'Donnell: Okay, we can recommend “redwood:audit”. Do you typically set source/host too?

[03:35] Jordan Lee: Yes. I’d suggest host like “redwood-inference” or “redwood” and source like “redwood:audit:export”. If customers have multiple workspaces/tenants, you can put tenant_id in the event body and use it in searches.

[03:49] Kevin Osei: We include workspace_id / tenant_id at the top-level. Also environment like prod/staging if configured.

[03:57] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[04:00] Colin O'Donnell: What about index-time extraction? Do we want to instruct customers to do props/transforms or just rely on KV_MODE=json?

[04:08] Jordan Lee: Prefer search-time extraction. Set props.conf with KV_MODE=json for that sourcetype, and TIME_PREFIX / TIME_FORMAT if needed. Avoid heavy transforms unless you have to for CIM.

[04:22] Maya Patel: For time: if you send ISO-8601 in a consistent field, Splunk can pick it up, but it’s safer to specify.

[04:28] Kevin Osei: Our field is event_time, RFC3339/ISO-ish, like 2025-01-29T17:59:58.231Z.

[04:37] Jordan Lee: Great. Then in props you can do something like TIME_PREFIX = "event_time" or use TIME_FORMAT=%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3NZ. The exact syntax, we can send you a snippet.

[04:52] Colin O'Donnell: That would be super helpful. We’re writing a partner-facing guide and a customer setup guide.

[04:58] Evan Brooks: Also, consider setting TRUNCATE=0 if you’re worried about long events getting cut.

[05:04] Jordan Lee: True, but be careful. TRUNCATE=0 can allow huge events that hurt parsing. If your events are bounded, that’s less scary.

[05:12] Kevin Osei: We can keep a max size and drop to DLQ if it exceeds. We already have a poison-pill concept.

[05:18] Jordan Lee: That’s good.

[05:20] Colin O'Donnell: Let’s talk about delivery semantics and duplicates, because customers ask. We’re at-least-once end-to-end. In some failures, we can resend and customers might see duplicates in Splunk.

[05:33] Jordan Lee: That’s standard. If you have a unique event_id, customers can do dedupe in searches or in correlation rules. In Splunk ES, correlation searches can do stats values by event_id, or use transaction, but transaction is heavy.

[05:47] Maya Patel: We typically advise a lookup-based dedupe for high-volume feeds, but that’s more advanced.

[05:53] Kevin Osei: For our schema, event_id is UUID. We also have “export_id” maybe? I’m blanking on the exact name.

[06:00] Colin O'Donnell: It’s destination_id and a delivery attempt id internally. In the payload we’ll have event_id, tenant/workspace, event_type, actor, target, and request context.

[06:12] Jordan Lee: If you can include a stable “event_hash” it can help, but honestly event_id is enough.

[06:19] Kevin Osei: We also include a schema_version so parsing is stable.

[06:23] Jordan Lee: Great.

[06:25] Colin O'Donnell: Now field mapping. You mentioned CIM alignment. What do you see as the minimal mapping so that Splunk ES can do something useful without lots of transforms?

[06:37] Jordan Lee: CIM has data models like Authentication, Change, Network, etc. For audit logs, it’s mostly Authentication and Change/Configuration. If you can map:
- user / src / dest / action / status
- app / vendor_product
Then ES dashboards will light up more.

[06:55] Kevin Osei: Our actor has actor.type (user, api_key, service), actor.id, actor.email sometimes, and actor.ip. We have request.ip and request.user_agent.

[07:06] Maya Patel: You probably want src_ip = actor.ip or request.ip. But in service-to-service calls, actor.ip might be null.

[07:13] Kevin Osei: Yep, request.ip is the best. Actor.ip exists for interactive.

[07:18] Jordan Lee: So recommendation: always send request.ip as a top-level field too, not nested too deep.

[07:23] Kevin Osei: It’s currently request.ip. We could also duplicate as source_ip, but we were trying not to proliferate.

[07:31] Jordan Lee: If you keep it nested, Splunk can still extract it, but some ES content expects src. You can use FIELDALIAS at search-time to map request.ip to src.

[07:42] Colin O'Donnell: So you’d suggest we provide a “field alias stanza” in the setup guide rather than changing the schema.

[07:48] Jordan Lee: Exactly. Keep your schema clean. Provide optional props.conf snippets:
FIELDALIAS-src = request.ip AS src
FIELDALIAS-user = actor.email AS user
Stuff like that.

[08:02] Maya Patel: Also vendor_product. That helps in ES.

[08:06] Kevin Osei: We have service.name = redwood-inference maybe. And event_source.

[08:12] Jordan Lee: Right. If you can include vendor=Redwood and product=Inference, or vendor_product="Redwood Inference".

[08:20] Colin O'Donnell: Okay.

[08:22] Jordan Lee: For change events like RBAC, you want “object” and “object_category”. CIM uses “object” sometimes.

[08:30] Kevin Osei: Our target is target.type and target.id. Like target.type="rbac_role" target.id="admin" or resource IDs.

[08:40] Jordan Lee: Good. Then alias target.id AS object, target.type AS object_category.

[08:49] Colin O'Donnell: Let’s do a quick walkthrough of an example event and you can tell us what you’d tweak.

[08:55] Kevin Osei: Sure. Example: user_login event. Fields: event_id, event_time, event_type="auth.login", outcome="success" or "failure"; actor: {type:"user", id, email}; request: {ip, user_agent}; workspace_id; region; and maybe mfa_used.

[09:18] Jordan Lee: That’s pretty good. For ES, having outcome as success/failure can map to “action” and “status”. Like action=login, status=success. You can either send those or alias them.

[09:31] Maya Patel: Also, if you have session_id, it’s useful. If not, no worries.

[09:35] Kevin Osei: We have session_id in some contexts, but not universal.

[09:40] Evan Brooks: Another one is “app”. Like app="Redwood Console" vs API.

[09:46] Colin O'Donnell: We have actor.client maybe? Hmm. We have request.route sometimes.

[09:51] Kevin Osei: We can include “surface” like console/api/sdk. It’s not in v1 yet, but could be.

[09:58] Jordan Lee: If it’s not stable, don’t add just for Splunk. But if you already have it, it’s helpful.

[10:04] Colin O'Donnell: Got it.

[10:06] Jordan Lee: For parsing: Splunk will auto extract nested JSON but sometimes the dotted field names become weird, like request.ip becomes request.ip (fine), but some apps expect src. Again, alias solves.

[10:18] Kevin Osei: On HEC payload format: do you prefer we use the HEC envelope fields (time, host, source, sourcetype) and put the audit JSON under “event”?

[10:28] Jordan Lee: Yes. That’s the standard: {"time":..., "host":..., "sourcetype":..., "source":..., "event":{...}}. If you set time as epoch, Splunk uses it. If you keep event_time in the inner event, Splunk can still use it but may set _time differently.

[10:44] Kevin Osei: We currently do both sometimes. We can set HEC time to event_time epoch.

[10:49] Jordan Lee: That’s ideal.

[10:51] Colin O'Donnell: One nuance: we support batching. We’re posting an array of HEC events per request.

[10:58] Jordan Lee: That’s fine. Splunk accepts multiple JSON objects separated by newlines, or a single payload with multiple events depending on your implementation.

[11:07] Evan Brooks: The newline-delimited JSON objects is common.

[11:10] Kevin Osei: Yep, we’re doing NDJSON.

[11:13] Jordan Lee: Great.

[11:15] Colin O'Donnell: Any gotchas with Splunk Cloud vs Enterprise for HEC?

[11:21] Jordan Lee: Cloud endpoints are different hostnames, sometimes behind LB. But functionally: token, endpoint, ACK if enabled. Also rate limiting is real—HEC will throw 429 or 503. Your connector should back off.

[11:35] Kevin Osei: We classify errors as auth (401/403), throttling (429), retryable (5xx), and permanent schema errors.

[11:44] Jordan Lee: That’s good. On 503 from Splunk, exponential backoff with jitter. And maybe a circuit breaker so you don’t hammer.

[11:53] Colin O'Donnell: We’ve seen retry storms in staging. We’re adding backpressure.

[11:58] Maya Patel: Another piece: if a token gets rotated, you’ll see 401/403. Your UI should surface the error clearly.

[12:06] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, our Console shows per-destination status: last_success, last_error, and an error id.

[12:12] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[12:14] Colin O'Donnell: Switching to field mapping suggestions—could you propose a small mapping table we can recommend? Like “if you want ES, add these aliases.”

[12:25] Jordan Lee: Yes. Off the top:
- event_type -> signature or action (depends)
- outcome -> status
- actor.email -> user
- request.ip -> src
- target.id -> object
- workspace_id -> tenant or vendor_account (some folks map to “vendor_account”)
- region -> vendor_region
- actor.type -> user_type maybe

[12:47] Kevin Osei: For workspace_id, we call it “workspace_id” consistently. Some customers say tenant_id. We can provide both? Or alias.

[12:55] Jordan Lee: Alias is fine. Don’t duplicate. But you can document.

[13:00] Maya Patel: Also add “dest” if there’s an API endpoint. Like request.host or request.path.

[13:06] Kevin Osei: We have request.path and request.method. And request.request_id.

[13:12] Jordan Lee: Great. That’s helpful for investigations.

[13:15] Colin O'Donnell: Let me pause—are we missing anything you’d expect from a vendor audit feed?

[13:21] Jordan Lee: Two things: consistent naming and examples. And ensure you don’t include secrets. Like API key value shouldn’t show, only key id.

[13:29] Kevin Osei: Absolutely. We only log key_id and last4. No raw tokens.

[13:35] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[13:37] Fatima Noor: For regulated customers, they always ask about encryption in transit. Splunk HEC with TLS—anything else we should mention?

[13:44] Jordan Lee: TLS 1.2+, validate certs. Don’t disable verification. If they have a proxy, just ensure SNI works.

[13:52] Fatima Noor: Got it.

[13:54] Colin O'Donnell: We also support mTLS in some private cases, but not in beta.

[13:58] Jordan Lee: If not, don’t claim it.

[14:02] Colin O'Donnell: Cool.

[14:04] (crosstalk)

[14:06] Kevin Osei: One more detail on ACK. If ACK polling times out, we treat it as retryable. That can create duplicates.

[14:13] Jordan Lee: Yes. That’s okay if your event_id is stable. Again, customers should handle duplicates.

[14:20] Kevin Osei: Do you see customers trying to “prevent duplicates” in Splunk?

[14:25] Jordan Lee: Sometimes they try, but it’s hard at ingest. Better is detection logic dedupe.

[14:32] Colin O'Donnell: Understood.

[14:34] Colin O'Donnell: Okay, we’re going to jump around a bit. There’s also the question of index naming and retention. Customers often ask: should audit logs go in a dedicated index?

[14:45] Jordan Lee: Yes, ideally. Separate index helps retention policies and access controls. Some customers put it in a “security” index with restricted roles.

[14:54] Maya Patel: And then create a role for SOC analysts with read access.

[14:57] Colin O'Donnell: Great.

[15:00] Jordan Lee: Also, if you’re doing Splunk ES, they like normalized fields. But you can get to “good enough” with your raw JSON plus a few aliases.

[15:10] Colin O'Donnell: Makes sense.

[15:12] Kevin Osei: Can you talk about sourcetype granularity? One sourcetype for all Redwood audit events, or per category like redwood:audit:auth, redwood:audit:admin?

[15:23] Jordan Lee: Keep it one sourcetype unless there’s a strong reason. You can use event_type for category filtering. Too many sourcetypes becomes a maintenance headache.

[15:33] Kevin Osei: Okay.

[15:34] Colin O'Donnell: Cool. Then we’ll stick with one.

[15:38] Jordan Lee: You can still have tags, like tag=authentication if you want via event_type-based tagging. But that’s optional.

[15:46] Colin O'Donnell: Understood.

[15:48] (brief pause)

[15:50] Colin O'Donnell: I want to make sure we capture the actual HEC “recommended config” list. Let me read back what I heard, and you correct me.

[15:57] Colin O'Donnell: 1) Create dedicated HEC token scoped to a security index. 2) Use TLS only, validate certs. 3) Prefer enabling HEC ACK if sender supports it. 4) Set sourcetype=redwood:audit, set host/source consistently. 5) Use search-time JSON extraction (KV_MODE=json) and specify TIME_FORMAT if needed. 6) Use field aliases to map to CIM-ish fields like src/user/status/object. 7) Keep batch sizes moderate; handle 429/503 with backoff.

[16:26] Jordan Lee: That’s basically it.

[16:28] Maya Patel: Add: avoid index-time transforms unless necessary.

[16:31] Colin O'Donnell: Great.

[16:33] Kevin Osei: Do you recommend gzip compression on HEC requests?

[16:38] Jordan Lee: If Splunk supports it in your environment, yes. But some proxies break it. So maybe optional. If you do, set Content-Encoding: gzip.

[16:49] Colin O'Donnell: Ours is optional, we can keep off by default.

[16:53] Evan Brooks: For Splunk Cloud it generally works, but test.

[16:57] Colin O'Donnell: Great.

[17:00] Colin O'Donnell: Can we talk about example SPL? Like what would you show a customer to validate things are working.

[17:07] Jordan Lee: Simple validation:
index=security sourcetype=redwood:audit | head 20
Then:
index=security sourcetype=redwood:audit event_type="auth.login" | stats count by outcome
And maybe:
index=security sourcetype=redwood:audit event_type="rbac.change" | table _time actor.email target.id outcome

[17:30] Kevin Osei: That’s great. We can include that.

[17:33] Colin O'Donnell: Also, for troubleshooting 401/403, would you search for errors from the connector, but those are on our side.

[17:40] Jordan Lee: Right. On Splunk side, they can check HEC metrics/logs, but typically they just see missing events. So your destination health view is important.

[17:49] Colin O'Donnell: We have that.

[17:51] Jordan Lee: For Splunk Cloud, there’s also an “HEC health” page, but customers don’t always have access.

[17:58] Colin O'Donnell: Makes sense.

[18:00] (The conversation continues with detailed Q&A; key excerpts below)

[18:12] Kevin Osei: For RBAC change events, do you care about old vs new values?

[18:16] Jordan Lee: It’s useful, but not mandatory. If you include a diff object like {"added":..., "removed":...} it’s helpful. But keep it small.

[18:26] Kevin Osei: We have changes: {"from":..., "to":...} for some settings.

[18:31] Jordan Lee: That’s fine.

[19:04] Maya Patel: On field names: try to keep snake_case, Splunk handles it well. Avoid spaces or weird punctuation.

[19:11] Kevin Osei: We’re snake_case.

[20:02] Evan Brooks: If you want to help customers in ES, provide a simple macro or saved search for “Redwood Audit Overview”.

[20:10] Colin O'Donnell: Nice idea. We can include as optional.

[21:15] Colin O'Donnell: Quick question: do you see customers requesting HEC raw endpoint versus event endpoint?

[21:20] Jordan Lee: Event endpoint. Raw is if you’re sending plain text. JSON goes to event.

[22:03] Kevin Osei: What about Splunk’s “line breaking” issues?

[22:07] Jordan Lee: If you’re using HEC event endpoint with proper JSON, line breaking isn’t your problem. That’s more for file-based inputs.

[23:18] Colin O'Donnell: Good.

[24:40] Jordan Lee: One thing: advise customers to turn on “Index acknowledgement” and configure a reasonable ack polling timeout. If your connector retries too aggressively, you’ll cause duplicates and load.

[24:54] Kevin Osei: We’re thinking ack polling max 30 seconds per batch, then treat as unknown and retry with backoff.

[25:02] Jordan Lee: That’s fine.

[26:37] Fatima Noor: Some of our private deployment customers have egress restrictions and ask for Splunk forwarder instead of HEC.

[26:44] Jordan Lee: That’s common, but for your beta, HEC is simplest. If they want forwarder, that’s a different integration.

[26:51] Fatima Noor: Yep, we’re not doing forwarder in beta.

[28:05] Colin O'Donnell: There’s also a question about Splunk HEC indexes: does it matter if they’re using SmartStore, etc.

[28:11] Jordan Lee: Not for you. That’s storage tiering.

[30:22] Colin O'Donnell: Okay. We should talk about “shared field mapping suggestions” as a tangible output. Jordan, can you send a mapping list, even a rough one, after this?

[30:31] Jordan Lee: Yeah, I’ll draft a simple table: Redwood field -> CIM-ish field -> notes. We’ll keep it minimal.

[30:40] Kevin Osei: And I’ll send you our “minimum guaranteed fields” so you don’t map to something that’s optional.

[30:46] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[32:10] Maya Patel: Also, think about geolocation. If you include country/region from IP, Splunk can do it too, but if you already have it, it helps. Just label it clearly.

[32:20] Kevin Osei: We have request.geo.country and request.geo.region sometimes, derived server-side.

[32:27] Jordan Lee: Great. Alias to something like src_country, src_region if you want.

[34:55] Colin O'Donnell: Anything else we should bake into the exporter defaults? Like sourcetype default.

[35:00] Jordan Lee: If you can set sourcetype by default, do it. Customers like “it just works.” But let them override.

[35:08] Colin O'Donnell: We do allow override in destination config.

[36:42] Kevin Osei: On PII: do customers ever want email addresses? That’s PII technically.

[36:48] Maya Patel: They usually do for investigations. The key is: don’t include secrets, and allow filtering. Email is acceptable in most enterprise audit logs.

[36:57] Kevin Osei: We’ll keep email for user actors when present.

[38:05] Colin O'Donnell: Great. I think we have enough.

[38:08] Jordan Lee: One last note: Splunk HEC has a concept of “channel” header for load balancing and ACK. If you support it, set it stable per destination.

[38:18] Kevin Osei: We do set a channel header. It’s a UUID per destination.

[38:22] Jordan Lee: Great. That helps.

[39:40] Colin O'Donnell: Let’s do recap and next steps.

[39:44] Colin O'Donnell: Kevin will share the minimum field list and a couple of example events (login, api key rotate, rbac change). I’ll send a proposed sourcetype/host/source recommendation and sample SPL queries. Jordan will send a CIM-ish mapping table and suggested FIELDALIAS stanzas. Then we’ll schedule a short follow-up.

[40:05] Jordan Lee: Sounds good.

[40:07] Maya Patel: Works.

[40:08] Evan Brooks: Yep.

[40:10] Colin O'Donnell: Awesome. Thanks all.

(Recording ended)
